tldr: A method that automatically synthesizes diverse and controllable dexterous manipulation policies in simulation without dense human demonstrations, by optimizing and chaining sparse static hand-object interaction templates to target object shapes and refining them into physically plausible behaviors using residual reinforcement learning.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of DexLink. Taking target object waypoints and sparse interaction templates as input, it generates a closed-loop control policy via three steps: (1) object-aware retargeting, (2) creating a reference trajectory by interpolating between waypoints, and (3) refinement using residual reinforcement learning in simulation.
overview:
Dexterous robot manipulation with multi-fingered hands involves complex contacts, making teleoperation and motion data collection by humans exceptionally difficult. This scarcity of diverse training data has been a major bottleneck. Conventional simulation-based approaches also face a dilemma: either rely on dense human demonstration data (such as motion capture or video) or use reinforcement learning with simple generic rewards. However, the former lacks scalability because it requires demonstrations for every specific object, while the latter cannot intentionally control finger-object contact patterns or fine-grained execution timing.

To solve this, the authors developed DexLink, a framework that synthesizes diverse behaviors by chaining sparse, reusable hand-object interaction templates as keyframes. First, it maps (retargets) templates to the target object geometry while preserving spatial relationships, and interpolates them along target object waypoints to build an approximate reference trajectory. Although this reference ignores physical laws and contact dynamics, residual reinforcement learning (Residual RL) in simulation automatically corrects dynamical discrepancies and contact offsets, turning it into a robust closed-loop policy.

Experiments spanning diverse tasks—including single-hand, bimanual, articulated objects, and dynamic handovers—demonstrate that the same templates can be flexibly reused across object scales and categories. They also confirm that users can control execution speed, grasp poses, and high-level strategies as intended. Furthermore, policies trained purely in simulation were deployed zero-shot to a real XHand robot, successfully achieving grasp-and-lift tasks.
contributions: Building DexLink, a simulation-based framework that synthesizes diverse dexterous manipulation behaviors from sparse hand-object interaction templates and object state waypoints.

Proposing an object-aware retargeting method that adapts poses to varying object geometries while simultaneously preserving hand configuration and relative hand-object spatial relationships (using BPS descriptors).

Refining approximate geometric reference trajectories into physically feasible closed-loop policies using residual reinforcement learning, enabling fine-grained behavioral control across four axes: target pose, interaction type, timing, and high-level strategy.

Demonstrating the reusability of interaction templates through extensive experiments spanning single-hand, bimanual, articulated, and dynamic tasks, along with successful zero-shot deployment to a real robot.

sections.heading: The Dilemma of Dexterous Manipulation Data and the Goal of DexLink
sections.summary: Learning dexterous multi-fingered manipulation requires diverse data, but human teleoperation is costly and standard RL struggles to precisely control contact behaviors. DexLink resolves this trade-off by combining sparse, reusable hand-object interaction templates with target waypoints to build coarse reference trajectories and refining them via residual reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
Dexterous multi-fingered manipulation by robots involves rich contacts and high degrees of freedom, making it extremely difficult to collect large amounts of demonstration data through teleoperation. While simulation-based synthetic data generation holds great promise, existing approaches face two main challenges.

The first is the reliance on dense human demonstrations (motion capture or video annotations). While this easily produces intended motions, it requires demonstrations for every specific object and task, limiting scalability. The second is reinforcement learning (RL) using generic reward functions. Although easily applied across diverse objects, it cannot control delicate fingertip contact patterns or timing, often leading to unnatural motions.

### Synthesizing Behaviors from Sparse, Reusable Representations
DexLink takes as input sparse, modular representations: object state waypoints (sequences of target positions and orientations) that define task progression, and hand-object interaction templates placed at key task waypoints. These templates can be sourced from existing static hand-object datasets or single frames of motion capture, and are reusable across object scales and categories.

The input templates are optimized to match the target object geometry (object-aware retargeting) and interpolated between waypoints to create a reference trajectory. Even though this reference lacks physical validity, using it to guide residual reinforcement learning narrows the search space while refining it into a physically feasible, closed-loop policy. This eliminates the need for expensive dense demonstrations and task-specific reward engineering.

captions.F2: Relationship between task specification and generated behavior. (a) By specifying an object path for a cup (lift -> flip -> place) and two interaction templates (grasp poses), (b) DexLink synthesizes a physically plausible closed-loop control policy satisfying them in simulation.

sections.heading: Limitations of Prior Work: Reliance on Dense Demonstrations and Uncontrolled Contacts
sections.summary: Prior work on dexterous motion generation broadly falls into four categories: RL reward design, dense demonstrations, grasp generation, and retargeting techniques. However, each has shortcomings regarding contact diversity, dynamic tasks, or geometric adaptability.
sections.details:
Here is an overview of prior research lines and how DexLink overcomes their limitations.

### Generating Dexterous Demonstrations
Methods that craft RL reward functions generalize well to unseen objects, but they cannot precisely control fingertip-object contact patterns and require substantial reward engineering effort for each task. Conversely, methods capturing dense demonstrations from teleoperation, mocap, or video allow fine control, but the data collection cost is prohibitive and hard to scale to new objects. DexLink achieves the best of both worlds by placing sparse static templates only at critical waypoints and leaving interpolation and physical refinement to RL.

### Grasp Generation and Scalability to Dynamic Tasks
While generating grasp poses from interaction templates is widely studied, approaches based on force closure or generative models cannot be directly applied to tasks involving continuous, dynamic contact transitions such as flipping or handovers. DexLink uses analytical optimization to generate approximate grasp poses first, resolving dynamic contact changes downstream via residual RL.

### Human-to-Robot Retargeting
Traditional retargeting methods mapping human hand poses to robot hands typically preserve only fingertip positions or finger vector geometries. However, when object geometry changes, this causes fingers to penetrate the object or miss target contact surfaces. DexLink introduces object-aware retargeting by incorporating relative spatial relationships with the target object mesh directly into the optimization objective.

sections.heading: From Rough References to Precise Control: A Two-Stage Motion Synthesis Pipeline
sections.summary: DexLink follows a clear pipeline: defining task specifications, constructing reference trajectories via object-aware retargeting, and refining them with residual reinforcement learning. Optimization handles variations in object geometry, and residual RL corrects rough geometric trajectories into physically sound controllers.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Specification
A task specification consists of a sequence of target object state waypoints (positions, orientations, and joint angles) $\mathcal{G} = \{\mathbf{s}_{0}, \mathbf{s}_{1}, \dots, \mathbf{s}_{K}\}$, and hand-object interaction templates $\psi_k$ assigned to specific waypoints. A template contains the source object mesh $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{src}}$, hand keypoints $P^{\mathrm{h}}$, and a rotational alignment to the target object $R^{\mathrm{src} \to \mathrm{tgt}}$.

### 3.2 Reference Trajectory Construction (Retargeting and Chaining)
The reference trajectory itself does not need to be dynamically feasible; it only needs to guide the RL exploration in the right direction. This involves two steps:

- **Object-Aware Retargeting:**
  Optimizes the robot's wrist pose $\mathbf{w}_k^\star \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ and joint angles $q_k^\star$. The objective is the sum of a hand configuration loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cfg}}$ that preserves geometric finger arrangements, and a hand-object relational loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ that maintains spatial relations between hand keypoints and the object surface. The relational loss uses differentiable Basis Point Set (BPS) descriptors combining distance, displacement direction, surface normal, and normalized object coordinates, enabling accurate transfer even for non-contact states like handovers.
- **Waypoint Chaining:**
  Robot poses at each waypoint are interpolated in accordance with object motion. Translations and joint angles use linear interpolation, while rotations use spherical linear interpolation (SLERP). After an interpenetration resolution step, a time-indexed reference trajectory $\xi_t$ is constructed.

### 3.3 Refinement via Residual Reinforcement Learning
Using the reference trajectory $\xi_t$ as a base, a closed-loop residual policy $\pi_\theta$ is trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in simulation.

- **Residual Action:** The policy receives the current robot state, contact sensor values, object state, and reference state $\xi_t$, and outputs bounded corrections (residuals) to the reference wrist pose and finger joint angles, executed by low-level PD controllers.
- **Reward Formulation:** In addition to a sparse task-completion reward, dense rewards include object tracking ($r_{\mathrm{obj}}$), wrist and finger reference tracking ($r_{\mathrm{ref}}$), interaction pattern preservation ($r_{\mathrm{int}}$), and a joint acceleration smoothness penalty ($r_{\mathrm{smooth}}$).
- **Trajectory Resets:** To parallelize long-horizon task learning, initial states are sampled from arbitrary timestamps along the reference trajectory upon environment resets. This allows all task phases to be learned simultaneously and efficiently.

sections.heading: Broad Task and Object Adaptability, and Sim-to-Real Deployment
sections.summary: Evaluations across diverse simulated tasks (single-hand, bimanual, articulated, dynamic) demonstrated that templates transfer across object scales and categories, providing fine-grained behavioral control. Ablations highlighted the necessity of reference trajectories and residual formulations, and zero-shot transfer was validated on a real XHand.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
The 5-fingered XHand (ROBOTERA) was used as the robot hand. Interaction templates were extracted from the OakInk and ARCTIC datasets. Drake (SNOPT) served as the optimization solver, and the Genesis simulator (with 1,024 parallel environments) was used for RL. Policies were trained across 3 random seeds for 51.2 million environment steps each.

### Key Findings
- **Retargeting Quality:** Retargeting 287 interactions across 33 categories from OakInk satisfied force closure in approximately 60% of cases at a 1 cm contact threshold and 80% at 2 cm, while preserving the diversity of pose distributions in PCA space.
- **Robustness to Object Geometry Variations:** In mug and bottle lifting tasks, the same templates were transferred to 4 scales (0.75x to 1.25x) and different instances/categories. The policy achieved 100% success across 13 out of 20 conditions near nominal scale, showing high adaptability without object-specific demonstrations.
- **Fine-Grained Behavioral Control Axes:** Altering task specifications along four axes—target pose (cup tilt angle), interaction type (bottle side vs. top grasp), timing (hammer swing speed), and high-level strategy (block pushing vs. lifting)—yielded success rates of 66% or higher across all variations. Varying swing speed intentionally controlled impact force from ~4 N to ~7.5 N.
- **Ablation Studies:** Baselines without hand reference trajectory optimization, using delta actions without references, resetting only from the initial state, or omitting interaction rewards showed severe performance drops on long-horizon tasks like notebook opening or block stacking. Providing reference trajectories for both wrist and finger joints and learning residuals proved crucial.
- **Comparison with Dense Trajectory Tracking:** In dense tracking experiments using ARCTIC mocap data, DexLink achieved comparable or superior tracking performance (ADD-AUC metric) without requiring manually designed gravity or velocity curriculums as in prior work.
- **Real-Robot Validation (Sim-to-Real):** Point-cloud policies trained purely in simulation with domain randomization were deployed zero-shot to the real XHand. The policy successfully achieved 6 to 9 lifts out of 10 trials, not only on training objects (mug, mustard bottle) but also on unseen objects (blue cup, Lego block).

captions.F9: Zero-shot grasp-and-lift experiments on a real robot (XHand). Point-cloud policies trained in simulation were transferred directly to hardware, achieving high success rates (6/10 to 9/10) on both seen training objects (mug, mustard bottle) and unseen objects (blue cup, green block).

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: DexLink establishes a framework that synthesizes diverse, controllable multi-fingered manipulation behaviors with high fidelity by chaining sparse hand-object interaction templates and combining them with residual RL. Future work includes automating task specification generation and expanding to deformable objects.
sections.details:
This paper presented DexLink, a framework capable of synthesizing a wide spectrum of dexterous behaviors—including single-hand, bimanual, articulated object, and dynamic manipulation—by chaining sparse static hand-object interaction templates with object state waypoints.

Experiments confirmed fine-grained behavioral controllability across target pose, contact type, timing, and strategy, template reusability across object sizes and categories, and the viability of zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. This offers a clear path toward overcoming the primary obstacles in autonomous dexterous manipulation: the high cost of collecting demonstrations and the difficulty of controlling reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Appendix: Retargeting Formulation and RL Implementation Details
sections.summary: The appendix details the mathematical formulation of geometric hand losses (vector orientations, palm normals) and differentiable BPS-based relational losses, as well as residual RL hyperparameters and reward weight configurations.
sections.details:
### Formulations of Hand Configuration Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cfg}}$) and Relational Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}$)
The hand configuration loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cfg}}$ compares directional finger vectors, inter-finger vectors, and palm normal vectors derived from three palm points between the human and robot hands. Cosine distance is used for normalized vectors, and squared Euclidean distance for unnormalized vectors.

Meanwhile, the hand-object relational loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ introduces a differentiable BPS descriptor softly weighted by the minimum distance from hand keypoints to the object surface point cloud. Summing four error terms—distance, displacement direction, surface normal, and normalized object feature coordinates—accurately preserves both contact interfaces and non-contact spatial arrangements. Optimization completes in about 10 minutes on a single CPU core and is run only once offline prior to task execution.

### Interpenetration Resolution and RL Hyperparameters
Because retargeted poses may contain slight penetrations, a sequential line search per finger joint group is applied as post-processing to eliminate interpenetration while securing contacts.

For residual RL, 1,024 parallel environments are run in Genesis, with a 3-layer MLP of 256 units for the policy network. The normalized dense reward balances object tracking (weight 0.30), wrist tracking (0.15), finger tracking (0.10), interaction preservation (0.25), and smoothness (0.20), accompanied by a large sparse reward upon task completion.

captions.F11: Hand keypoint arrangements referenced across retargeting and reward computation. Color-coded markers denote corresponding joint locations between the human hand (left) and the multi-fingered XHand (right), used to measure agreement in finger directions and palm normal vectors.
captions.F12: Distribution of retargeting computation time (in minutes) across object categories. The average runtime is approximately 10 minutes on a single CPU core, representing a practical one-time preprocessing cost before reinforcement learning.

takeaways: The input formulation of 'sparse static contact templates + object waypoints' provides a practical alternative that drastically cuts the cost of collecting dense video or mocap demonstrations.

The two-stage design—building a coarse geometric reference trajectory via retargeting and absorbing dynamical discrepancies and contact timing through residual RL—is highly effective for stabilizing exploration while maintaining control precision.

Including finger joint motions in the reference trajectory and predicting them as residuals, rather than learning finger articulation from scratch, is decisive for succeeding in long-horizon, contact-rich tasks.

Capturing relative hand-object spatial relationships in a differentiable manner via BPS descriptors enables the reliable transfer of contact patterns across differing object geometries and categories.
limitations: Task specifications (object waypoints and template assignments) must still be explicitly provided, falling short of full end-to-end automation directly from raw video.
Real-robot validation was limited to grasp-and-lift tasks; real-world efficacy for bimanual coordination and articulated object manipulation shown in simulation remains to be verified.
The framework currently targets only rigid objects and does not handle deformable objects such as cloth or ropes.
